t: Leetcodify Friends Recommendations — Symmetric Pair Mining with an Anti-Join
o: From the listening log we must recommend users to each other: emit ordered pairs (user_id, recommended_id) in BOTH directions whenever two distinct users listened to at least three different songs on the same day and are NOT already friends. Walking Example 1: users 1 and 2 share songs 10, 11, 12 on 2021-03-15 but are friends, so they produce nothing; users 1-3 and 2-3 share those same three songs and are not friends, yielding the four recommendation rows; user 4 shares only songs 10 and 11 with user 1, and user 5 listened on a different day, so neither qualifies. Two data quirks drive the design: Listens may contain duplicate rows (count DISTINCT songs, never raw rows), and Friendship stores one orientation per pair while exclusions must test both orientations.
k: Deduplicate plays (or use COUNT(DISTINCT song_id)) so repeated listens cannot inflate the three-song threshold.
A self-join of Listens on (day, song_id) with differing user ids naturally emits both directions of each qualifying pair.
Friendship must be excluded via an anti-join (NOT EXISTS) that checks the stored pair in both orientations.

a.n: Approach 1: Correlated Counting Per User Pair
a.i: Cross join the distinct users to enumerate every ordered candidate pair, discard pairs connected by Friendship, then run a correlated subquery counting the distinct songs both users played on the same day. Keep only pairs reaching three. This is the most literal translation of the requirements and is easy to verify, though it rescans the log for every pair.
s: CROSS JOIN distinct user ids from Listens to form ordered pairs l1.user_id <> l2.user_id.
Filter out pairs present in Friendship in either orientation using NOT EXISTS.
Correlated subquery: join Listens a (user 1) with Listens b (user 2) on same day and song, counting DISTINCT song ids.
Keep pairs whose shared-song count is at least 3.

c.python:
# LeetCode SQL problem - Python driver not applicable.
# SQL solution:
"""
SELECT l1.user_id AS user_id,
       l2.user_id AS recommended_id
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM Listens) l1
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM Listens) l2
WHERE l1.user_id <> l2.user_id
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM Friendship f
      WHERE (f.user1_id = l1.user_id AND f.user2_id = l2.user_id)
         OR (f.user1_id = l2.user_id AND f.user2_id = l1.user_id))
  AND (
      SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT a.song_id)
      FROM Listens a
      JOIN Listens b
        ON b.user_id = l2.user_id
       AND a.day = b.day
       AND a.song_id = b.song_id
      WHERE a.user_id = l1.user_id
  ) >= 3;
"""

a.t: O(U^2 * L) — every ordered user pair triggers a co-listen scan over L log rows
a.sp: O(L) — deduplicated user set and join buffers

a.i: Share the pairing work: join Listens to itself on matching day and song for distinct users, group by (user pair, day), and require COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) >= 3. Because the join is symmetric over all rows, both recommendation directions emerge automatically. A final NOT EXISTS strips pairs that are already friends. Grouping by day as well prevents two weaker days from being summed into one qualifying day.
s: Self-join Listens l1/l2 on equal day and song_id with l1.user_id <> l2.user_id.
GROUP BY user pair and day; HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) >= 3.
SELECT DISTINCT the resulting ordered user pairs so multiple qualifying days collapse to one row.
Anti-join against Friendship testing both orientations.

c.python:
# LeetCode SQL problem - Python driver not applicable.
# SQL solution:
"""
SELECT DISTINCT t.user_id,
       t.recommended_id
FROM (
    SELECT l1.user_id AS user_id,
           l2.user_id AS recommended_id,
           l1.day AS day,
           COUNT(DISTINCT l1.song_id) AS shared
    FROM Listens l1
    JOIN Listens l2
      ON l1.day = l2.day
     AND l1.song_id = l2.song_id
     AND l1.user_id <> l2.user_id
    GROUP BY l1.user_id, l2.user_id, l1.day
    HAVING shared >= 3
) t
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Friendship f
    WHERE (f.user1_id = t.user_id AND f.user2_id = t.recommended_id)
       OR (f.user1_id = t.recommended_id AND f.user2_id = t.user_id));
"""

a.t: O(L^2) — the self-join materializes co-listen row pairs before grouping
a.sp: O(L^2) worst case for the grouped intermediate result

w: Lead with the grouped self-join; keep the correlated version as a readability fallback for small tables. Pitfalls: forgetting bidirectionality (the sample output contains both (1,3) and (3,1)); grouping without the day column, which lets 2+1 songs across two days fake a qualifying day; counting raw joined rows instead of DISTINCT songs when Listens holds duplicates. MySQL accepts the alias in HAVING; portable dialects repeat the COUNT expression. Follow-up: sibling problem 1919 flips the logic to REQUIRE friendship and reports canonical user1_id < user2_id pairs.
